source.title: A suite of Vision Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The post reports vision-SAE training and reconstruction MSE by image-token position, but does not test dark-matter structure, predictability, or scaling across SAE sizes.
record.gate_note: The reported layer-20 monosemanticity result does not bear on the claim. The token-position reconstruction-MSE finding is recorded under fits_no_version because it does not test the cross-size predictability asserted in V2.
record.test_reason: The post releases vision top-k SAEs and reports only autointerp by layer and per-token-position reconstruction MSE. It does not measure linear predictability of error, cross-size error scaling, loss effects versus random errors, or functional use of the error term. It also does not compare architectures as a test of dark matter. It does not cite the dark-matter paper.
record.authors_conclusion: This is mostly right. The authors call their findings preliminary and not rigorous. They report layer 20 as the most monosemantic layer by sort-eval autointerp, with the most frequently active features. They say outer tokens are easier to reconstruct than middle tokens, presumably because middle tokens carry richer foreground information. The record's paraphrase omits the layer-20 finding.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains top-k SAEs for vision-transformer interpretation but does not investigate or reproduce a dark-matter analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: The post says outer image tokens are easier to reconstruct than middle tokens throughout training, for CLIP ViT-L top-k SAEs. It gives no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision-transformer SAEs, reconstruction error varies systematically with image-patch position.

record.problems: The authors say the analysis has not been demonstrated to a high degree of rigor. The supplied text gives no numerical MSE values or uncertainty estimates for the plots and reports no controls.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from input activations.
Error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
Downstream loss of spliced reconstructions compared with random errors of the same norm.
The split between linear (unlearned-feature) and nonlinear dark matter.
Whether circuit or steering analyses need the error term.
Whether dark matter shrinks with different architectures or training objectives.

record.verdict_notes: This is a resource release post on LessWrong. Figures are not in the text, and no numerical MSE values are given. There are no dark-matter analyses.

versions.untested_parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from input activations.
Error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
Loss effects of SAE reconstructions compared with random errors of the same size.
The proposed distinction between unlearned-feature and nonlinear dark matter.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose model behaviour unless the error term is retained.
Whether dark matter is an SAE-training artifact or shrinks with different architectures or end-to-end training.

rows.subject: laion/CLIP-ViT-L-14-laion2B-s32B-b82K
rows.operation_detail: Measured reconstruction MSE for image tokens across SAE training.

conditions.value: all 257 image tokens were trained; CLS token excluded from the plotted comparison

rows.value: Outer tokens were easier to reconstruct than tokens in the middle.
rows.note: The post describes plots across tokens and training, but supplies no individual numerical MSE values in the text. This is an aggregate statement across layers.
rows.check: The row's link to none is correct. It holds a single SAE size per layer, so it cannot bear on V2's cross-size predictability. It reports no numbers, only a qualitative statement from plots. The state 'observed' describes the post's own finding, not any version, so it is set to cannot_determine relative to the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
